channel.title: Open Indus News
channel.description: New and landmark research on the Indus script, summarised.

item.title: An open test for filling in missing signs
item.description: Many seals are chipped, so some signs are lost. This team trained a model to fill the gaps and published everything: the code, how they split the texts for training and testing, and the model's guesses. Because it is all open, anyone can check how good it really is. What we take from it: We graded it. 36% of its test texts have a near-copy in its training texts. On clean texts the neural model does no better than a simple three-sign model (28.5% vs 29.8% right on the first guess).

item.title: One sign that never follows another
item.description: Most of the paper's grammar gain is tiny. But it makes one clear claim: a certain sign never comes right after the arrow sign, yet often comes right after the jar sign. A rule that sharp is easy to test on texts the author did not use. What we take from it: We tested it. The pattern shows in reading order on the main texts, but not on texts kept aside, and gaps this sharp are common: 24 of 57 similar sign pairs have one. So it is real but not special.

item.title: A fair way to ask “is this a language?”
item.description: Is the Voynich manuscript a hidden language, or meaningless copying? The authors write each explanation as a machine that produces text, give both machines the same amount of tuning, and score them on pages kept aside. They checked the method on 28 texts in 16 languages and on planted messages. What we take from it: The equal-effort, held-out rule is now our standard for any reopened “language or code” test.

item.title: An invented symbol system with no sounds looks just like the Indus script
item.description: He built an artificial system of emblems with no language behind it. It matched the Indus script on every measure he could compute exactly. Programs that “decode” by matching dictionaries happily read it as English, Sanskrit or Tamil. So those numbers cannot settle whether the Indus signs write a language. What we take from it: Every new claim we test must also fail on SIGIL-style emblem data. We use it as a standing negative control.

item.title: The Indus script sits between coats of arms and paperwork
item.description: The author built artificial sign systems of different kinds, such as coats of arms and office records, and compared their statistics with the Indus texts. The Indus script lands between the two. What we take from it: Agrees with our finding that each kind of object has its own vocabulary. Nothing new to run.

item.title: Reported: a new seal with Indus signs from the UAE
item.description: A news site reports a small round seal of the Gulf type, with Indus signs and a humped bull, from Umm al-Quwain. The excavation report, the exact find spot and a readable photo of the signs have not been published, so we cannot use it yet. What we take from it: We looked for an excavation report and found none, and the news page is now offline. It stays out of our data until the find is published.

item.title: The “registration code” reading fails its own predictions
item.description: This preprint argued that seal texts are like registration numbers: each one unique, with numbers in fixed places. We ran their tests on 646 Mohenjo-daro unicorn seals. The texts turned out less unique than chance, and the number patterns did not hold. What we take from it: Nothing to borrow. Their best result was already known, and the rest fails.

item.title: The full edition of Linear Elamite, the script read through kings’ names
item.description: Linear Elamite, from what is now Iran, was read in 2022. The key was royal names already known from cuneiform, on objects dated well enough to predict which names should appear. This book publishes the full set of texts from Susa. What we take from it: We used Linear Elamite as a known-answer test for our own name-matching method. The method could not recover its values, so we stopped it rather than run it on Indus.

item.title: India’s archaeology agency held a three-day meeting on the script
item.description: The Archaeological Survey of India brought researchers together for three days to review where decipherment stands. Only the programme is public so far. What we take from it: We have asked the agency whether readings proposed there can be scored on our open test bench.

item.title: Teaching computers to find signs and animals in seal photos
item.description: The team trained image models to find the signs on a seal photo, name each one, and recognise the animal. Only sample data is public. The full set is available from the authors on request. What we take from it: Reading signs straight from photos could settle the 1-in-5 disagreements between the two main transcriptions. We need open images first.

item.title: Do Indus signs look more like scripts from the Himalayas than from Mesopotamia?
item.description: Using image AI, the authors compare sign shapes and report that scripts from the Tibetan-Yi corridor, such as Naxi Dongba and Yi, look more like Indus signs than proto-cuneiform or Proto-Elamite do. Looking alike does not mean sounding alike, but their open sign images are useful. What we take from it: We red-teamed it. The claim technically survives, but its whole edge comes from one small script, Ba-Shu. Proto-cuneiform is closer to Indus than four of the five Himalayan scripts.

item.title: 15,184 marks on South Indian pottery, many with Indus look-alikes
item.description: Archaeologists in Tamil Nadu catalogued 15,184 marks scratched on pots from 140 sites and found that most have an Indus sign that looks similar. The marks are about 1,000 years younger, and most stand alone rather than in texts. What we take from it: We tested whether look-alikes behave alike. They do not, so this route is closed for now.

item.title: How computers are opening up Proto-Elamite, the Indus script’s unread neighbour
item.description: Proto-Elamite, from Iran, is unread and about as old as the Indus script. Teams have used computers to learn how its texts are organised: which signs start an entry, which complex signs are made of simpler ones, and which counting system each number belongs to, by looking at what is being counted. None of this needs the language. What we take from it: We tried the pieces that fit. Indus signs that look like Proto-Elamite or proto-cuneiform signs do not behave like them (0 of 5 tests), complex signs do not split into their parts, and no known number system matches the Indus counts. Still untried: letting a model find genres from scratch.

item.title: Linear Elamite read, through kings’ names
item.description: The team read Linear Elamite by finding the names of kings they already knew from cuneiform, written on silver beakers that could be dated. Each name gave the sounds of several signs. The Indus script has no such object yet: no text in a known script that names an Indus person. What we take from it: This is why we search for names of people from the Indus region in cuneiform records, and asked museums for seal impressions on tablets that name them.

item.title: Letting the computer decide which shapes are the same sign
item.description: Scholars disagree about whether two similar shapes are one sign or two. For Cypro-Minoan, this team let a model look at each sign’s picture and where it appears, and group them. The Indus script has the same problem: the two main sign lists count about 400 and about 700 signs. What we take from it: Build an Indus sign list the same way, starting from the open glyph images, and see which version of the list the data prefer.

item.title: The texts as labels for goods and permits, not names
item.description: Mukhopadhyay reads the inscriptions as practical labels: what a parcel holds, how much, and who may pass, rather than people’s names. Stroke signs would be units whose value depends on the goods, and some signs would stand for crops or other commodities. In 2025 she proposed the fish signs mean gems. What we take from it: A first test found no sign tied to a craft at two sites, but it had too little data to tell. The fish = gem prediction needs find spots from bead workshops, which we have asked excavators for.

item.title: DNA from Rakhigarhi: who the Indus people were
item.description: Scientists read the DNA of a person buried at the Indus city of Rakhigarhi. It had no ancestry from the Eurasian steppe, which arrived in South Asia later, and it is related to the main ancestry of later South Indians. That fits an Indus language that was not Indo-European, perhaps related to Dravidian, but genes do not prove a language. What we take from it: Background only. It narrows the likely language families but gives no sign values.

item.title: Computers can crack a script, if they know a related language
item.description: Machine learning re-cracked two ancient scripts: Ugaritic, matched against Hebrew, and Linear B, matched against early Greek. The trick only works when you already know a closely related language. For the Indus script, no such language is known. What we take from it: We tested the planted-language version at Indus size. Without the right language, it fails, so this route waits for an outside clue.

item.title: Indus signs used in a new way on seals from the Gulf
item.description: Traders around Bahrain made round seals of their own style but carved Indus signs on them. Laursen showed these seals use the signs differently, for example often putting a “twins” sign at the front. One explanation is that local names were written with borrowed signs. What we take from it: Our round-seal finding builds on this, and adds that round seals found in Indus cities break the order too.

item.title: Does sign order prove it is a language? The numbers say no
item.description: Rao’s team measured how predictable the next sign is and found the Indus script sits in the same band as languages. Sproat replied that symbol systems that are not writing can score the same way, and that two better measures put Indus with non-writing. Later work, including SIGIL, settled it: these numbers alone cannot decide. What we take from it: Treat entropy, Zipf and n-gram arguments as closed in both directions.

item.title: The case that the signs might not be writing at all
item.description: The authors pointed out that Indus texts are very short, about five signs on average, that many signs appear only once, and that no long text has ever been found. They argued the signs could be a system of symbols, like road signs or coats of arms, rather than writing that records speech. What we take from it: We test whether the signs are language at all, instead of assuming it.

item.title: The best-known case that the signs write an early Dravidian language
item.description: Parpola argues the signs are mostly word-signs that also work like puns, the way a picture of a bee plus a leaf can spell “belief”. His famous example is the fish sign: in Dravidian languages the word mīn means both fish and star, so a number plus fish could name a star group. What we take from it: We turned his readings into predictions and tested them. Six + fish holds as a fixed unit; “seven stars” is not supported; the fish signs group together but do not behave like god names.

item.title: The list of every text that made the field possible
item.description: Mahadevan drew every sign, gave each a number and listed every known inscription, with every place each sign appears. Almost all statistical work since, including ours, starts from this list. What we take from it: The backbone of our main transcription.

item.title: Reading Maya history before reading a single sound
item.description: Maya monuments carry dates. Proskouriakoff noticed that the dates on each group of monuments spanned a human lifetime, and that the same glyphs always sat beside a first date (birth) and a later one (taking the throne). So the texts were about real rulers. She worked out what glyphs meant from the pattern of events, years before anyone could read their sounds. What we take from it: We tried one version: seals from the same house share no more signs than seals from nearby houses. Still untried: seals broken on purpose, buried with someone, or found at gates.
